card.hook: Some mornings Table Mountain pulls a cloud over its flat top like a tablecloth, and you're left standing there waiting for it to lift. Check the forecast and bring a little patience, because the wait is often worth it.
card.stand_here: Go to Signal Hill and stand at the quieter small car park near the top, or on the hiking path that leads from it, not the main upper car park. Face the mountain and you'll see it side-on, with its cliffs and flat top, Lion's Head alongside and fynbos at your feet.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to take in the whole scene. Switch to 0.5x to get the fynbos up close and Lion's Head in the same shot, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the cliffs and the straight edge of the plateau.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and sit the top edge of the plateau on one of the horizontal lines so it stays dead straight.
card.best_time: Sunrise is the recommended time for this view, and the small car park is quieter then. If you go for sunset, arrive early because parking fills up.
card.selfie_here: Stand inside the big yellow metal picture frame on Signal Hill with Table Mountain behind you. Use the front camera and try 0.5x so the mountain peeks over your shoulder, and Lion's Head shows in the frame too.
card.ask_someone: On Tafelberg Road in front of the lower cableway, stand with the steep mountain face filling the background and ask a passer-by to take your photo.
card.rules_and_safety: Casual photos for personal use don't need a permit. Be careful not to fall when taking selfies at the spots on top of the mountain, and remember parking is limited near sunset.
card.challenge: Get the plateau edge perfectly straight with a strip of fynbos along the bottom, then see if you can catch the cloud spilling over the top.
card.good_to_know: The flat top is roughly three kilometres from side to side and edged by steep cliffs, with Devil's Peak to the east and Lion's Head to the west. It stands about 1,000 metres above the streets below. It also holds around 2,285 plant species, about 80% of them fynbos.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go to Signal Hill and stand at the quieter small car park near the top, or on the hiking path that leads from it, not the main upper car park. Face the mountain and you'll see it side-on, with its cliffs and flat top, Lion's Head alongside and fynbos at your feet.

card.hook: Picture four scoops of almost-white sand, each tucked between giant round granite boulders, with Lion's Head standing guard behind. You get the best look at all of it from up high, where it's quieter than down on the sand.
card.stand_here: Head to The Rock, at the end of Ocean View Drive, and walk from the parking spots to the point near it. Face south and look down on the Clifton beaches and the boulders between them.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the beaches and boulders in together. Go 0.5x if you want more coast and sky, or 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out one beach or the pattern of the boulders.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and put the line of the beaches along the lower third, then tap the sand and drag the brightness down a little so the white doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day and check the weather before you set off, because haze and cloud flatten the sea colours. Late summer gives you the widest beaches, while in winter the sand is stripped back and the boulders stand out more.
card.selfie_here: Go down to Clifton 4th Beach and sit on one of the granite boulders at the cove, with the white sand and sea behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a little low and keep the beach over your shoulder. It's lovely there at golden hour.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the steps above the cove at Clifton 4th Beach and shoot down while you stand on the sand, so the cove and boulders fill the frame (late morning is best, before the beach fills up).
card.rules_and_safety: Stay on the walking path from the parking spots and don't climb onto the boulders or out to their edge. It can be windy up there. If you try Kloof Road, it's a busy winding road, so keep to the pavement or a safe verge. Check the official site and local signs for any parking or access restrictions.
card.challenge: Use a boulder in the foreground to lead the eye down the coast, then see if you can get all four beaches into one shot.
card.good_to_know: Clifton is four small beaches, numbered 1st to 4th from north to south, split by big granite boulders. They're well sheltered from the strong south-easter, which is part of why they're so popular. Fourth Beach is the busiest and most glamorous, and it has Blue Flag status.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to The Rock, at the end of Ocean View Drive, and walk from the parking spots to the point near it. Face south and look down on the Clifton beaches and the boulders between them.

card.hook: Most spots make you hunt for the perfect angle. Here, someone has built a giant yellow picture frame and pointed it straight at Table Mountain, so the hard part is already done.
card.stand_here: Head to the big Yellow Frame on the harbour side, near the Den Anker restaurant. Stand at the frame and face Table Mountain, with the harbour and city skyline behind you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the mountain fills the frame naturally. Switch to 0.5x for more frame and sky, or 2x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to bring the mountain closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line the mountain up with the middle of the frame, and tap the mountain, then slide the picture a little darker if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day when Table Mountain isn't hiding under cloud. Go early if you want fewer people in your picture.
card.selfie_here: For a Waterfront landmark behind you, stand on Clock Tower Bridge right in front of the red-brick Clock Tower. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the tower peek over your shoulder. The Yellow Frame near Den Anker is built for selfies too, but it's Table Mountain behind you there, not the Waterfront.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photos are generally fine here, but commercial photography needs a permit, and security can be strict about professional gear. The Waterfront is described as one of Cape Town's safer areas, even at night, because it's well-lit and patrolled.
card.challenge: Take one clean shot of the mountain sitting perfectly centred in the frame with a dead-level horizon, then swap places with your travel buddy and do it again.
card.good_to_know: The V&A Waterfront sits on the oldest working harbour in the Southern Hemisphere. It began in 1654, when Jan van Riebeeck built a small jetty here to supply passing ships. The two harbour basins were built between 1860 and 1920, and the Clock Tower, built in 1882, now leans very slightly.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the big Yellow Frame on the harbour side, near the Den Anker restaurant. Stand at the frame and face Table Mountain, with the harbour and city skyline behind you.

card.hook: Most cable cars make you fight for the window. This one turns the floor under your feet, so everyone gets a turn at the view without moving an inch.
card.stand_here: Stand by a window inside the Table Mountain Aerial Cableway cabin. The phone icon on the map is halfway along the route, so this is a ride-time photo. Face outwards and shoot the scene as it slides past.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the view, the mountain and your fellow passengers into one frame. Switch to 1x for a cleaner shot of a single scene, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for details like Robben Island or the city blocks below.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the scenery outside, not the glass, then slide it a touch darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day, because cloud can hide the view. Morning or late afternoon is worth trying for softer light and slightly fewer people.
card.selfie_here: At the top, try the small balconies off the WiFi Lounge windows at the upper cable station, which a reviewer says have wide views. Use the front camera at 0.5x, hold your arm out and keep the big view over your shoulder. I can't promise the cable car itself will be in the shot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on Roeland Street, facing the lower cableway station, to frame you so the whole station fits in the shot behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Casual photos for personal use don't need a permit, but follow any posted photography rules. The summit is exposed and flat, and wind can whip across it with little shelter, so hold your phone tight.
card.challenge: Take three frames as the floor turns: the city, then the sea, then the rock face, and see which one you'd frame.
card.good_to_know: The cableway opened on 4 October 1929 and has been upgraded three times since. The current 'Rotair' cars date from 1997 and hold 65 passengers each. The ride takes about five minutes and ends at the upper station, 1,067 metres up. Check the official site before you go, as weather and operating changes can affect it.

card.hook: Sea, white sand, a jagged wall of mountain and a row of cafés, all in one shot. Camps Bay hardly makes you work for it.
card.stand_here: Start at Camps Bay Viewpoint, the free roadside terrace that's open all the time and sits higher than the sand. Face the bay so the beach curves below you and the Twelve Apostles ridge fills the top of your frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole bay, beach and mountains in. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the ridge or Lion's Head on a clear day.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the mountains, then slide the brightness a little darker so the sky keeps its colour and the sand doesn't turn white.
card.best_time: Go at sunrise or golden hour, when the light is at its kindest. Sunset is a favourite at the viewpoint too. Opinions differ on which end of the beach looks best, so have a quick look around when you arrive.
card.selfie_here: At Camps Bay Viewpoint, use your front camera and stand with the bay and Lion's Head over your shoulder. For a calmer backdrop, try the tidal pool at the end of Camps Bay Beach with the Twelve Apostles behind you. Zoom 0.5x helps fit more mountain in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to take your photo from the sand at the northern end of Camps Bay Beach, with the Twelve Apostles rising behind you, ideally in late afternoon light.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay off the rocks at Camps Bay Viewpoint and stick to the safer ground of the terrace. Parking nearby can be hard at busy times, so allow a bit of extra time.
card.challenge: Get sea, sand, mountain and sky all in one frame, with a strip of beach along the bottom, then see if you can spot Lion's Head.
card.good_to_know: Camps Bay Beach is the largest white sand beach in the area and has been a Blue Flag beach since 2008. Victoria Road was finished in 1887. In 1901 a tramway started bringing visitors out for the day, along with tidal pools and a pavilion for concerts.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start at Camps Bay Viewpoint, the free roadside terrace that's open all the time and sits higher than the sand. Face the bay so the beach curves below you and the Twelve Apostles ridge fills the top of your frame.

card.hook: Pink, red, blue, green and purple houses stand shoulder to shoulder here, and the street climbs so steeply that the rows seem to step up the hill. Bo-Kaap is made for phone photos, and the colour does most of the work for you.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Wale Street and Chiappini Street, on the diagonal corner of the intersection. Face down the hill, and you'll get two rows of coloured houses meeting at the corner, with Table Mountain at the far end on a clear day.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the corner itself. Try 2x if your phone has it, which helps you pick out one row of houses from the crowd. Save 0.5x for narrow lanes, and hold the phone level so the houses don't lean.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and put the corner where two grid lines cross, so the downhill street leads the eye to the mountain. If the colours look washed out, tap a bright wall and slide the brightness down a touch.
card.best_time: Go early, in the first two hours after sunrise. Tour groups tend to build up after about 8 am, so you'll have more room before then. A clear sky also gives you Table Mountain.
card.selfie_here: Try the pink house on the corner where Rose Street and Wale Street meet. One local blog calls it the most iconic colourful backdrop, and it usually has a vintage blue car parked out front. Use the front camera, hold it a little low, and let the house sit over your shoulder. The upper part of Wale Street is another good spot, with a row of coloured houses and Table Mountain rising behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand near the lower end of Wale Street and shoot uphill, while you stand a little way up with the houses climbing behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: People live here, so don't sit or lean on their steps, don't approach front doors, and ask before photographing residents. One guide advises against walking alone in Bo-Kaap after dark.
card.challenge: Can you get a shot with the corner on a grid crossing, Table Mountain at the end of the street, and nobody wandering through the frame? Patience is the secret ingredient.
card.good_to_know: Bo-Kaap is the oldest surviving residential neighbourhood in Cape Town, and it has the largest concentration of pre-1850 buildings in South Africa. In 2019, 19 sites here were declared National Heritage sites. The bright paint is often put down to a sense of freedom after emancipation, though the colourful look seems to date mainly from the late 20th century.

card.hook: This isn't a grand-view kind of stop. The star is an old Methodist church on a city street, and the best photo is of its plain, honest front.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, right at the District Six Museum building. Face the church and frame the whole front.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole church front in. If the pavement is narrow and you can't step back, try 0.5x, but keep your phone level so the walls don't lean. For a close-up of the doorway or signage, try 2x or 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the church's vertical edges up with them so the walls look straight.
card.best_time: Go in daylight, when the front of the building is evenly lit. A quieter moment helps too, so you can wait for a clear gap in the people and traffic.
card.selfie_here: The one named selfie spot is indoors, at the large floor map of the district in the main hall, where former residents wrote where their homes stood. The church won't be behind you there, so use the front camera and keep it simple, with the map as your backdrop. Be mindful of other visitors around you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is allowed inside, but please take photos respectfully given the sensitive history. Check the official site for photography rules before you start, and be thoughtful about photographing other visitors.
card.challenge: Can you get the church front perfectly straight against your gridlines, with a little pavement at the bottom and no one walking through?
card.good_to_know: The museum is both a museum and a memorial. It remembers the forced removal of about 60,000 people of various races from District Six during apartheid in the 1970s. The foundation behind it was set up in 1989, and the museum opened in 1994. Inside, the floor map carries handwritten notes from former residents, and there are old street signs and displays about family life and the demolition.

card.hook: Picture a huge stadium sitting between a mountain and the sea, like someone parked it in the best spot in Cape Town. From up on Signal Hill, that's exactly what you get.
card.stand_here: Head to the Signal Hill lookout area, on the hill above Green Point (you reach it by the Signal Hill road). Face down the hill so the stadium sits below you against Table Bay, with Table Mountain and the city bowl behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to catch the whole scene of stadium, bay and mountain. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pull the stadium and mountain closer together. Use 0.5x only if the hillside in front adds something, because the stadium will look small.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the stadium, then slide the brightness down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the mountain doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: The hour before sunset is often said to give the best light. After dusk, switch on night mode and rest your phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the Sea Point promenade, starting at Mouille Point on Beach Road. Face the ocean with your front camera and the stadium should be behind you, then go to 0.5x to squeeze in more of the scene over your shoulder. (This is our best reading of the guides, so have a look around and adjust.)
card.ask_someone: Out on the Breakwater at the V&A Waterfront, ask a passer-by to take your photo while you stand with the stadium in view across the harbour water; it's a lovely misty-afternoon spot.
card.rules_and_safety: The stadium is a secured venue, so take your photos from public land outside the fence, and check the official site for event closures or photo rules before you go. The Signal Hill road can be busy, so pull in only where it's safe and legal.
card.challenge: Get the stadium, Table Mountain and the sea all in one frame, with the horizon dead level, and put the stadium on the lower third line of your gridlines.
card.good_to_know: Cape Town Stadium was built for the 2010 FIFA World Cup. Building began in March 2007 and took 33 months, and it was handed over to the City of Cape Town on 14 December 2009. It held 64,100 people for the World Cup, was later reduced to 55,000, and since 2021 it's been called the DHL Stadium for sponsorship reasons.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the Signal Hill lookout area, on the hill above Green Point (you reach it by the Signal Hill road). Face down the hill so the stadium sits below you against Table Bay, with Table Mountain and the city bowl behind it.

card.hook: Those thick yellow walls weren't painted for show. They were chosen to take the sting out of the heat and sun, and they look fantastic against Table Mountain.
card.stand_here: Head inside to the Oranje Bastion and stand on top of it, facing Table Mountain. The fort sits in front of you, with the mountain and Lion's Head rising behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the fort up front and the mountain behind. Try zoom 0.5x to fit in more of the star-shaped walls and sky, then zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pull Table Mountain and Lion's Head closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the castle walls in the bottom third, then tap the mountain and nudge the slider to darker so the sky keeps its colour and the yellow walls don't wash out.
card.best_time: Go soon after the castle opens, or in the softer light of late afternoon. Opening and closing times vary, and the castle can close for film shoots or private events, so check the official site first.
card.selfie_here: Try the Kat Balcony, next to the 'Kings of the Castle' sculptures, where Table Mountain is in view. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and hold it at arm's length, so you and the mountain both fit in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a friendly passer-by to stand in the middle of the outer courtyard and aim at the clock tower, while you stand in front of it so the yellow walls fill the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Don't take photos in the William Fehr Collection where signs forbid it, because flash damages the old paintings. Watch your footing on the ramparts if it has rained, and keep your phone safe once you leave the gates, as the area around the train station can be unsafe.
card.challenge: Can you get a yellow wall, Table Mountain and Lion's Head all in one frame, with no stranger's head sneaking in?
card.good_to_know: The Dutch East India Company built the castle between 1666 and 1679, and it is the oldest existing building in South Africa. It once stood on the shore of Table Bay, but land reclamation has left it inland. On weekdays, the Key Ceremony at 10am is when the Castle Guard formally opens the castle.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head inside to the Oranje Bastion and stand on top of it, facing Table Mountain. The fort sits in front of you, with the mountain and Lion's Head rising behind it.

card.hook: Squint a bit and Lion's Head turns into a crouching lion, with Signal Hill as its tail. The Dutch spotted it in the 17th century, and now it's your turn.
card.stand_here: Head for the broad grassy crest at the top of the road on Signal Hill. Face south-west, because Lion's Head is to your south-west, rising behind the city bowl, the harbour and the Atlantic seaboard.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the city, harbour and sea in with the mountain behind. Switch to 1x for a calmer, more natural look. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to bring Lion's Head closer so it looks bigger against the city.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the mountain, then slide the brightness down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the peak doesn't go flat.
card.best_time: Sunset is the popular choice here. Get there early, because parking is limited and fills up fast. For a different angle in early light, Kloof Corner looks across the gap to Lion's Head with Camps Bay below.
card.selfie_here: Try the Lion's Battery viewpoint on Signal Hill. A local guide says the hill gives a frame with both Table Mountain and Lion's Head, so use the front camera at 0.5x and keep Lion's Head over your shoulder. Or try the sand at Clifton 4th Beach, which is listed for its views of Lion's Head.
card.ask_someone: At the Lion's Battery viewpoint on Signal Hill, ask a passer-by to frame you with Lion's Head in view behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Parking on Signal Hill is limited. Lion's Head is in Table Mountain National Park, so check the official site before you climb it or fly a drone. Take care near the steep edges at Kloof Corner. One local blog suggests a guided hike rather than going alone at sunrise or sunset, because one way is in the dark.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines, put the lion's 'back' on an upper line, and get a strip of grassy ridge at the bottom for depth.
card.good_to_know: Lion's Head rises to 669 metres above sea level and sits between Table Mountain and Signal Hill. The Dutch called it Leeuwen Kop in the 17th century. It's part of Table Mountain National Park.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the broad grassy crest at the top of the road on Signal Hill. Face south-west, because Lion's Head is to your south-west, rising behind the city bowl, the harbour and the Atlantic seaboard.

card.hook: Picture an old concrete grain silo that's grown pillow-shaped glass windows near the top. That's Zeitz MOCAA, and it's hard to take a boring photo of it.
card.stand_here: Head to the Silo District at the V&A Waterfront, where the tall silo is easy to spot. The phone icon on the map is at the museum itself, so there's no extra walk. For the big shot, walk back along the Waterfront paths until the whole tower fits, then face the building.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x to get the full height of the tower in one go. Switch to 1x for general views, then 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to home in on the glass and concrete.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the tall edges of the tower with them, so the building stands straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light flatters the concrete and glass more than harsh midday sun. Check the museum's own site for visiting details.
card.selfie_here: Stand on Silo Square with the silo facade behind you, hold your phone at arm's length with the front camera, and keep as much of the tower in the shot as you can. Inside, the central atrium on the lower level is another good spot: tilt your phone up so the light shafts overhead are in the frame behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back on Silo Square while you stand in front of the museum entrance with the silo building behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is usually allowed, and restricted areas are marked with signs, so ask staff if you're unsure. Selfie sticks are typically not allowed inside the galleries. The rooftop sculpture terrace has glass floors over the silos below, which can be tough going if you don't like heights.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole tower, then find a bulging glass panel and fill the frame with it.
card.good_to_know: The silo was built between 1921 and 1924 and stands 57 m tall. Heatherwick Studio carved galleries and a tall central atrium out of its 42 tightly packed concrete cylinders. The museum opened on 22 September 2017 and has nine floors, a sculpture garden, a rooftop restaurant and a coffee shop, with The Silo Hotel in the upper part of the tower.

card.hook: Cape Town has a hill that looks like it's lying down for a nap next to a lion. From the Sea Point promenade you get the classic low view: sea in front, Sea Point's buildings in the middle, and flat-topped Signal Hill rising behind.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Sea Point promenade, right on the sea-front at street level, so there's no climb. Face south-east and Signal Hill and Lion's Head rise side by side above the coastline.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the sea, the hill and Lion's Head all in one shot. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the hill closer. The 0.5x button gives you lots of sea and sky, but the hill will look small.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the hill's skyline on the upper third line and the sea wall or promenade along the lower third.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day and go early or later in the afternoon, when the light is softer and it's quieter. If you head up to the summit for sunset, arrive early, because it gets very crowded and parking is limited.
card.selfie_here: The one selfie spot we can back up is the top of the Lion's Head hike, on the partly concrete surface at the summit, where Signal Hill is one of the views. We can't confirm the exact framing, so use the front camera, hold it a little low and a bit out, and see if the hill sneaks in over your shoulder. That climb isn't a casual stop, since it involves ladders and chains.
card.ask_someone: If you're on the Lion's Head trail, find a spot with Signal Hill in view and ask a passer-by to frame you with the ridge behind you (this one is a best guess, so check the view first).
card.rules_and_safety: Stick to populated areas and go with other people if you can. For the summit road, parking and the Noon Gun, check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take a frame with people walking into the scene for scale, and keep the promenade rail or lamp post out of the corners.
card.good_to_know: Signal Hill has a long working history. Flags were once used to send weather warnings and anchoring instructions to ships in the bay, and a time ball was set up here after 1836 so ships could check their clocks. The Noon Gun still fires daily at midday, except Sundays. The hill is also one of the only places where the rare Peninsula Shale Renosterveld vegetation survives.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Sea Point promenade, right on the sea-front at street level, so there's no climb. Face south-east and Signal Hill and Lion's Head rise side by side above the coastline.

card.hook: Picture rows of colourful craft stalls with a grand 18th-century building standing behind them like it's supervising the shopping. That's Greenmarket Square, and old and lively sit side by side here.
card.stand_here: Stand in the square in front of the Old Town House, facing its facade. Frame the building from the square rather than standing right up against it, so the stalls sit in front of it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the Old Town House with the stalls in front. If the crowds leave you no room to step back, tap 0.5x. For the building's details or the little hand pump, try 2x to 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines to keep the building's vertical lines straight, and let the stall colours fill the bottom of your frame.
card.best_time: Go mid-morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer. It's a busy market, so expect people in your shots. One blog says it's closed on Sundays, so pick another day.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie in front of the Old Town House's front door on the square. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and tilt up a little so the building is over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Burg Street where it opens onto the square, while you stand in the square with the Old Town House on the right of the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: There are no official restrictions on photography for personal use, but ask before taking close-up portraits of stallholders. One traveller advised being wary around Long Street and Greenmarket Square, though others felt safe, so keep an eye on your phone and bag.
card.challenge: Find the hand pump near the middle of the square and get a close-up of it. Then hunt down the most colourful stall and frame the pump and the stall in one shot.
card.good_to_know: The square began with a burgher watch house in 1696, and the Old Town House replaced it in 1761. Over the years the square has been a slave market, a vegetable market and a car park. Today it's a flea market, and the Old Town House holds the Michaelis Collection of art.

card.hook: Look up. Long Street's Victorian balconies repeat down both sides like a row of iron-lace piano keys, and with Table Mountain peeking over the rooftops, you get a big Cape Town hit in one frame.
card.stand_here: Stand on the pavement in the middle of Long Street, facing the heritage doorway of the Long Street Baths at the top (south-west) end. Cars only run uphill here, so they come up behind you. Keep to the pavement and watch the traffic.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the long view down the street. Switch to 0.5x when you're close to a building and want a whole balcony from bottom to top. Try 2x to pull Table Mountain closer behind the rooftops, if your phone has it.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the street up with a vertical line so the buildings don't lean, then tap the sky or the mountain and drag the brightness slider down a touch so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Go in the daytime when Table Mountain is clear of cloud, so peek at the sky before you set off. In the evening, switch on night mode and rest your phone against a wall or post to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Walk along Long Street itself and pick a spot with the painted Victorian-style building fronts, murals or street signs behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x so the street fits over your shoulder. If you fancy a change, Greenmarket Square's Old Town House door is a short walk away, but we can't promise Long Street shows in that shot.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay on the pavement, because traffic comes uphill from behind you. Guides also suggest watching for pickpockets, especially at night, so keep your phone tucked away between shots.
card.challenge: Once you've got the big view, hunt for three close-ups: a balcony, a mural and a street sign, then see if you can catch a passer-by walking through one of them.
card.good_to_know: Long Street is lined with bookshops, restaurants and bars, and has a lively, slightly bohemian feel. In the 1970s and 1980s several theatres here staged anti-apartheid plays, and most have since become restaurants or shops. The MyCiTi 101 bus runs the whole length of the street, with five stops along it.

card.hook: Stand in the middle of the Grand Parade and you might hear the City Hall clock chime the Westminster quarters, a very English sound for a very honey-coloured building. Let it be your cue to look up and start shooting.
card.stand_here: Stand on the open Grand Parade, across from Darling Street, with the City Hall about 2 minutes on foot to the south-west. Face the front facade so the whole building and clock tower fit in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the full facade and tower. Then go to 1x for a more natural look with less stretching at the edges. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the clock tower or the Mandela statue.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it stands straight, and keep your phone upright and level.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, when the eastern facade is fully lit and the wind is calmer. Peak summer afternoons can bring the Cape Doctor, a south-east wind that blows hard across the square.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the bronze Mandela statue at street level with the City Hall facade behind you, so the monument and the building fit together. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if your phone has it on the front. Sources disagree on where the statue stands (balcony or front of the building), so check on site first.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the open Grand Parade, across from the facade, and shoot back toward the City Hall while you stand in front of the building, with Table Mountain above the roofline if the air is clear.
card.rules_and_safety: Ask the security guard for permission before stepping inside the building to take photos. One reviewer advises visiting during the day and staying alert, as there can be beggars and unusual people nearby.
card.challenge: Get the clock tower perfectly straight on a gridline with a little sky above it, so Table Mountain peeks out behind. No leaning tower allowed!
card.good_to_know: Cape Town City Hall is an Edwardian building finished in 1905, built from honey-coloured limestone brought from Bath in England. On 11 February 1990, hours after his release from prison, Nelson Mandela made his first public speech from its balcony. A bronze statue of him now looks out over the Grand Parade.

card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x, which fits the lighthouse, the apartment blocks and Signal Hill all in one shot. Pinch to 2x if you want the tower bigger without moving. If you walk right up to the tower, try 0.5x to fit the whole thing in, and keep your phone level so the sides don't lean.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it stands straight, then tap the lighthouse and drag the slider to make it a little darker if the white stripes look washed out.
card.best_time: Morning light gives you the clean, graphic look. Late afternoon is also recommended, so pick whichever fits your day.

card.rules_and_safety: You don't need a ticket to photograph the outside from the park, but a visit inside may be ticketed or have restricted days and hours, so check the official site first. The area is considered safe, though some reviewers suggest keeping an eye on your belongings.

card.good_to_know: Green Point Lighthouse is a red-and-white lighthouse in Cape Town's Green Point area, close to the Waterfront promenade. Its stripes stand out against the modern apartment blocks around it. If you walk on to the lighthouse, you can turn around and shoot with the Waterfront promenade stretching out behind you.

card.hook: Picture rose beds in front of you and Table Mountain parked right behind them, all in the middle of a city. That's the Rose Garden in Company's Garden, and it's the best photo here.
card.stand_here: Head into the Rose Garden and stand among the beds. Face the way where Table Mountain shows up behind the roses (it's often visible, so look up and find it).
card.zoom: Start at 1x for roses with the mountain behind. Switch to 0.5x to squeeze more flowers into the foreground, or try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the mountain closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the skyline on the upper line so the roses fill the bottom, and crouch a little to make the flowers look bigger.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or late in the afternoon, when the light is softer. Midday sun is harsh. The roses look best in spring and summer, so winter beds may look a bit sparse.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie in the Rose Garden, right in the beds, with the blooms and greenery filling the frame behind you. For a Table Mountain backdrop, try the pathway beside the restaurant at 15 Queen Victoria Street. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the scenery over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The garden is free to walk through, and personal photos are generally fine. Professional shoots and drone use may need City of Cape Town permits, so check the official site first. If you photograph people up close, ask first.
card.challenge: Be patient and catch a squirrel, a dove or an Egyptian goose looking like it's posing for you.
card.good_to_know: Company's Garden is the oldest garden in South Africa. Dutch East India Company settlers started it in the 1650s to grow fresh vegetables for the settlement and for ships rounding the Cape. Master gardener Hendrik Boom prepared the first ground for sowing on 29 April 1652, and the Rose Garden came much later, in 1929.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head into the Rose Garden and stand among the beds. Face the way where Table Mountain shows up behind the roses (it's often visible, so look up and find it).

card.hook: Picture a row of columns standing in perfect lines, with leafy trees leaning in on both sides like they're trying to get into the photo. That's the back of South Africa's Parliament, and it's the calm, tidy side.
card.stand_here: Stand on Government Avenue at the edge of the Company's Garden and face the rear, garden-side façade across the avenue. The Parliament building is to the south-east, about 1 minute on foot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the façade framed by trees. If the whole width won't fit, tap 0.5x, and try 2x for a tighter shot of the columns.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines, line the columns up with the vertical lines so the building doesn't lean, and keep a tree trunk or branch on each side as a frame.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and gentler shadows between the columns. Check the light on the day, because the trees can throw patchy shade across the façade.
card.selfie_here: Try the Company's Garden lawns opposite Parliament, on the garden side, so the building sits behind you. Use the front camera, tap 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold it a little low so the building shows over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: For a photo of you both, ask a friendly passer-by to take it near the Parliament sign at the visitors' entrance on Plein Street (exact sign spot: check when you arrive), with you standing in front of the sign and them a few steps back.
card.rules_and_safety: Exterior photos are generally fine, but photography inside is restricted. Keep your phone away from the entrances and security staff, and follow any signs.
card.challenge: Count the columns in your frame, then see if your friends get the same number from your photo.
card.good_to_know: Cape Town is South Africa's legislative capital, while the government sits in Pretoria. The Houses of Parliament were built between 1875 and 1884. A fire in early January 2022 destroyed the National Assembly's session room, and the rebuild is targeted for June 2027, so the building may look a little different from older photos.

card.hook: Cross Wale Street, turn around, and there it is: a big Neo-Gothic front with both spires, filling your screen with warm stone. It's one of those spots where the building does all the work.
card.stand_here: Stand on Wale Street, on the pavement directly opposite the cathedral's front, facing the west front. The cathedral will be to the south-west of you.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x if you're close, so the whole front and both spires fit. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the windows, spires and carved stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line up the middle of the building with the centre line, and keep your phone level so the spires don't lean in.
card.best_time: Soft light early or later in the day usually suits the stonework better than harsh midday sun. The pavement also tends to be quieter early on.
card.selfie_here: Go up to the bronze cross at the top of the main entrance steps and face out toward Wale Street, so the cathedral should be behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and tilt up a little so the building fits over your shoulder. For a calmer backdrop, the courtyard garden next to the labyrinth is also a popular photo spot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the pedestrian St George's Mall, facing the cathedral across Wale Street from its main entrance, while you stand by the bronze cross.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a working place of worship, so photos may not be welcome during services or private events. Watch for traffic and people on the pavement, and keep clear of the entrance so you don't block anyone. The courtyard and labyrinth may be closed at times.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole front, then find one tiny stonework detail and see if a friend can guess where it is.
card.good_to_know: St George's is the Anglican cathedral of Cape Town and the seat of the Archbishop. Sir Herbert Baker designed it, with foundation stones laid in 1901 and the north transept finished in 1936. Desmond Tutu led marches from its front steps, which is why it's called the "people's cathedral", and it became a provincial heritage site in 2014.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Wale Street, on the pavement directly opposite the cathedral's front, facing the west front. The cathedral will be to the south-west of you.
